API authentication interpolates the raw X-APIKEY header into a glob pattern. Sending 'X-APIKEY: *' makes Path('/tmp/').glob('vulpy.apikey.*.*') match any existing key file, and the username is then returned from the file name - a complete authentication bypass (other metacharacters such as '?' work too). extra.message: CSRF on a state-changing GET endpoint: /mfa/disable turns off the victim's multi-factor authentication on a plain GET request, with no CSRF token and no OTP/password re-confirmation. A single embedded in any page (exactly the payload shipped in bad/payloads/hello.html) silently disables MFA for any logged-in victim whose browser renders it.

POST /user/chpasswd has no CSRF protection (no token, no origin/referer check), so a malicious page can silently submit a password change form for any logged-in victim and take over the account. The only guards are that the two fields match and the always-True complexity check.

The password change at /user/chpasswd never verifies the user's current password: libuser.password_change() updates the row by username alone. Anyone holding a stolen, forged, or CSRF-abused session can set a new password and permanently lock out the real account owner.

No rate limiting, throttling, or account lockout protects the login (the users.failures column created in bad/db_init.py:17 is never read or updated). Login credentials can be brute-forced without restriction, as demonstrated by the bundled tools bad/brute.py and utils/httpbrute.py. The same applies to the /api/key endpoint which calls the same login function.

extra.message: Logout never invalidates the session: the navbar 'LOGOUT' link merely navigates to /user/login, whose handler only pops the (unused) Flask session key. libsession.destroy() exists (bad/libsession.py:27-29) but is never called by any route, so the 'vulpy_session' cookie remains valid after logout and continues to authenticate the user on every subsequent request.

POST /user/create with username 'admin' inserts a second 'admin' row; libuser.login() then returns username 'admin' when presented with the attacker's password, so an attacker can impersonate any existing user, including admin.
